clue.text: Chips on the boards

parts.note: 'Chips' is the traditional nickname for a carpenter, and 'the boards' is the theatre stage, so this is the woodworker who builds scenery

explanation.surface: Wood shavings lying on a floor, or perhaps a snack dropped on the planks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chips' looks like fried potatoes or wood fragments, but it is the old nickname for a carpenter; 'treading the boards' means acting, so the boards are the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Chips is a nickname for a joiner, and one working in a theatre builds and shifts the scenery.

clue.text: Shorten a card-game

parts.note: bridge is a partnership card game for four players

explanation.surface: An instruction to cut short a hand of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a text is to cut it down to a shorter version.

clue.text: Get designs on copper?

parts.note: read not as scheming against a policeman but as engraving a pattern into a copper plate with acid

explanation.surface: Someone plotting against a police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have designs on' means to scheme to get something, and 'copper' is slang for a policeman; here it is literal, putting patterns onto the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Printmakers bite lines into a metal plate with acid to make an engraved image.

clue.text: A sweet sort of order

explanation.definitionFit: A fruit tart is a classic dessert, and 'apple-pie order' means perfectly neat and tidy.

clue.text: He throws vases etc — he needs the breaks

explanation.walkthrough: In snooker or billiards a break is a run of successive pots, so a potter at the table needs them; the surface suggests he needs rest periods.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceramicist throws clay on a wheel to make vessels, and in snooker a player sinking balls builds scoring runs called breaks.

clue.text: It grows dangerous to keep light away after dark

indicators.note: after places the shading piece second, behind the word meaning darkness

parts.note: after dark means at night, so dark stands for the night-time
to shade something is to shield it from light

explanation.surface: Something growing that becomes hazardous, sheltered from the sun after nightfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It grows dangerous' hides a plant: deadly nightshade, or belladonna, is poisonous.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadly nightshade (belladonna) is a toxic plant whose berries can kill.

clue.text: Sodium, I observe, is coming back for the schoolboy

indicators.note: coming back tells us the whole sequence of pieces is read from right to left

parts.note: Na is the chemical symbol for sodium
to note something is to observe it

explanation.surface: A chemistry pupil noticing that a sodium reading has returned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is coming back' turns the whole run NA + I + NOTE into ETONIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil at Eton College, the English public school, is called by this name.

clue.text: Distance from boarding-house to sea could be short in Weston

definitions.text: Distance from boarding-house to sea could be short in Weston

parts.words: Distance from boarding-house to sea could be short in Weston
parts.note: a seaside landlady's advertisement for a guesthouse close to the beach, the short distance being as far as a pebble can be flung

explanation.surface: A holiday advertisement promising lodgings near the beach at a seaside resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Weston-super-Mare is an English seaside resort full of boarding-houses; such places often claim to be very near the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a very small distance, as far as one could fling a pebble.

clue.text: Nut to break open on grass

parts.note: to crack a nut is to break it open
pot and grass are both slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: Instructions for opening a nut by smashing it on the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' means an eccentric person, not a kernel; grass is slang for cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are slang for an eccentric or crazy person.

clue.text: Spirit of general's first army

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: a host is an army or great multitude, as in the heavenly host

explanation.surface: The phantom of a general's leading regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit of the dead that walks is a spectre or apparition.

clue.text: Intensive programme of instruction for stock-car circuit?

explanation.walkthrough: Stock-car racing involves deliberate collisions, so its track could be called a course for crashes.
explanation.definitionFit: A short intensive training course has this name, and a stock-car track is literally a place where cars collide.

clue.text: Badger to sit up?

explanation.definitionFit: To pester someone is to keep on at them; sitting up on a horse or in a car is travelling.

clue.text: Train speed affected this sort of crossing

indicators.note: affected suggests the letters of the two words have been disturbed and rearranged

explanation.surface: A railway's speed has changed because of a level crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' and 'crossing' suggest a railway level crossing, but the type of crossing is the one with stripes for people on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A zebra crossing is a place on the road where walkers may cross.

clue.text: Feature of Scotland paradoxically dry ie., even so, inside

indicators.note: paradoxically signals that the word dry, against expectation, holds everything else within it
inside places the words before it within the word dry

explanation.surface: A Scottish landmark that is, oddly, abstinent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts STILL within IE; 'paradoxically' then sets that inside DRY, a nod to the paradox that a whisky distillery is anything but dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland is famous for whisky, made at many such distilling plants.

clue.text: Precise remedy

explanation.definitionFit: Something exact is particular, and a drug aimed at one disease is a targeted cure.

clue.text: Noises from coppers in narrow openings

explanation.definitionFit: Coins clinking together make a light ringing sound, and narrow cracks or gaps also go by this word.

clue.text: Casually release handles to impress?

parts.note: handles is slang for people's names, and letting them fall casually in talk is meant to impress listeners

explanation.surface: Someone carelessly letting go of door handles to show off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handles' looks like door knobs, but it is slang for names.
explanation.definitionFit: To mention famous acquaintances casually so as to impress others.

clue.text: Did his egg need a cruet, in parts?

definitions.text: Did his egg need a cruet, in parts?

indicators.note: in parts suggests the letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a clergyman's breakfast egg needed seasoning from the condiment set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A curate's egg' is something good in parts, from a Punch cartoon where a curate politely says his bad egg is good in parts.
explanation.definitionFit: An assistant clergyman is the figure in the cartoon whose egg was 'good in parts'.

clue.text: Burden to keep oneself from action

explanation.definitionFit: A burden is the chorus of a song, repeated lines; to abstain from doing something is also this verb.

clue.text: Couple of rounds, taking in course, for his lordship

explanation.walkthrough: A 'round' is a slice of bread; Sandwich in Kent is home to a famous golf course; the fourth Earl of Sandwich is said to have invented the snack.
explanation.definitionFit: Two slices of bread with filling, a golf course in Kent (Royal St George's), and the Earl who gave his title to the snack.

clue.text: The Man from Haifa" broadcast serial I follow

indicators.note: follow places the letter I after the rearranged word
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of the word are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Listening to a radio drama called The Man from Haifa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges the letters of 'serial' to make the country's name; 'follow' sets I after it. The stray quotation mark is in the source.
explanation.definitionFit: Haifa is a city in Israel, so a man from there is a citizen of that country.

clue.text: Describing Rosemary among the other ballerinas?

indicators.note: among tells us the letters lie within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A dancer called Rosemary in the company of fellow ballerinas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rosemary' looks like a girl's name, but it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosemary is a culinary plant, so an adjective for plants used in cooking or medicine applies.

clue.text: Wearing no head-band but retaining the bones

explanation.definitionFit: A fillet is a ribbon worn round the head, and fish that has not been boned still keeps its skeleton.

clue.text: Triplets in Beethoven's "Archduke," for example

explanation.definitionFit: A group of three, and Beethoven's Archduke is a well-known piano work for three players.

clue.text: Old-fashioned earth-deposit of valuable ore

indicators.note: fashioned means shaped or made anew, so the letters are remodelled

parts.note: E is the electrical abbreviation for earth

explanation.surface: An outdated description of a seam of precious mineral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old-fashioned' looks like one word meaning archaic, but it splits: 'fashioned' rearranges OLD with E.
explanation.definitionFit: A vein of metal-bearing rock in the ground is called this by miners.

clue.text: Fashion to become fit

explanation.definitionFit: To fashion something is to mould it, and someone getting fit is said to get into condition, in good form.

clue.text: Mortgagor not heeding Polonius?

explanation.walkthrough: Polonius is the counsellor in Shakespeare's Hamlet whose advice to his son includes not borrowing money.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone taking out a mortgage owes the lender money, and Polonius in Hamlet advises 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be'.

clue.text: Comprehensive knowledge Mac needs policy renewed

indicators.note: renewed suggests the letters are made over in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A man called Mac must get his insurance renewed.
explanation.definitionFit: Learning that covers every branch of knowledge, like a reference work of all subjects.
